system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2207-11-12 15:52:00 to 2207-11-20 17:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder with a suprapubic catheter, and a history of recurrent multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections, was admitted due to persistent fevers and malaise despite outpatient treatment with Bactrim for a suspected UTI. He presented with dizziness and weakness but no urinary symptoms. Initial evaluation showed no leukocytosis, and imaging revealed no abscess or obstructive uropathy. Urine culture grew Proteus mirabilis, resistant to Bactrim but susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. He was treated with IV antibiotics, transitioned to IV ceftriaxone, and discharged on oral cefpodoxime for a 10-day course. During admission, he was evaluated for dysphagia, with speech and swallow recommending a ground diet and supervised feeding. His stage II-III sacral and ischial pressure ulcers were managed with debridement and wound care, and plans were made for home support including a new mattress and cushion. Anemia and skin flaking were managed supportively. He was discharged home with services, stable and improving.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Pressure ulcer of sacral region, stage 3
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

Brief Hospital Course:
***anticipated length of stay in rehab less than 30 days***

___ with a h/o advanced MS, neurogenic bladder w/ indwelling

presented from home due to increased lethargy and fever.  He was 
found to have septic shock from urinary source, also with distal 
femoral fracture managed non-operatively.  His UTI was 
ultimately found to be due to a multi-drug resistant 
Pseudomonas, ultimately treated with Zosyn per infectious 
Disease.

ACTIVE ISSUES:
===============================
# Septic Shock due to UTI
Pt with a history of multiple UTIs (Pseudomonas, E.coli, 
Enterococcus, Klebsiella) with an admission UA showing WBC >182, 
positive nitrites. Also with a history of neurogenic bladder 
with indwelling suprapubic cath.  Initially required ICU 
admission, but quickly stabilized with low dose Levophed and IV 
fluids.  Other than urine, no other source of infection 
identified (see below - but his knee swelling was ultimately due 
to a fracture, and the arthrocentesis was a dry tap).  Urology 
exchanged the SPT catheter on ___.  He was initially on 
Vancomycin and Meropenem, later narrowed to Zosyn monotherapy.  
On ___, despite quick clinical improvement on Zosyn, speciation 
and sensitivities revealed a very resistant pseudomonas 
aeruginosa in the urine, and ID was consulted.  Despite 
""intermediate"" sensitivity to Zosyn, per ID recommendations, we 
did an extended Zosyn infusion time (over 3 hours).  He 
continued to remain hemodynamically stable.  PICC line was 
placed so he can complete a full 2 week course of Zosyn.  The 
last day of Zosyn is ___.

# Left distal femur fracture
Presented with knee swelling.  Xray showed impacted distal 
femoral metadiaphysis fracture with dorsal displacement and 
ventral angulation of the fracture apex. Ortho was consulted.  
It was felt to be likely subacute.  Ortho recommended hinged 
left knee brace, and follow up in clinic in 2 weeks.  
Arthrocentesis revealed a dry tap, so infection very unlikely.  
Continue brace and no weight bearing until ___ clinic 
appointment.

# Constipation:  Presented with significant constipation and 
stool burden on KUB.  Colorectal surgery was consulted, 
recommending daily tap water irrigation and aggressive PO bowel 
regimen.

# Multiple Sclerosis
Pt with suprapubic cath, which was changed on ___ by 
Urology. Continued oxybutynin.  He has a Baclofen pump which was 
due for a refill while admitted.  This was refilled by the 
Chronic Pain Service on ___ while he was here.

# H/o tobacco use - provided with nicotine patch

# Anemia:  Hgb 11.3 on admission, then down to mid-8's after 
IVF, likely due to dilutional effect.  It was subsequently 
uptrending.  Retic index low, likely hypoproliferative.  No 
gross evidence of bleeding.  Started iron supplement

# Sacral Decubitus Ulcer:  Wounds appear clear, well healing, no 
e/o infection.  Continued Vitamin C to promote healing.  Stopped 
Zinc, as this is usually done for a defined course only.

# H/o recurrent UTI's:  Has seen ID as outpatient, recently 
started on Macrobid.  Macrobid was stopped due to 
ineffectiveness.  He will follow up with ID as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your doctors here. You were brought in because your nurse noticed you were more lethargic than usual and you had a fever. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel tired… confused. My knee has been swollen for a few days, but it doesn’t hurt much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You have a fracture in your left femur near the knee. It’s not new, but there’s an acute component. We’re managing it with a brace for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fracture? But I didn’t fall. How did that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your multiple sclerosis and immobility, your bones are more fragile. Sometimes fractures can happen with minimal trauma or even just from shifting position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that makes sense. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but we don’t need surgery. Ortho recommends a hinged brace and no weight-bearing until your follow-up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. But why the fever and confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s from a urinary tract infection that led to septic shock. Your blood pressure dropped, so we gave fluids and a medication to support it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Septic shock? That sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but you’re responding well. Your blood pressure is stable now, and we’ve started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on vancomycin and meropenem for now. We’re waiting for urine culture results to see which bacteria is causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It’s Pseudomonas aeruginosa — a tough bacteria, especially with your history of resistant infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. The good news is it’s sensitive to piperacillin-tazobactam — we call it Zosyn. We’re switching to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the IV antibiotic I’m getting now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Because this strain is resistant to many drugs, we’re giving it over three hours each time to make it more effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. How long will I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About two weeks. We’ll place a PICC line so you can get it safely outside the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We changed your suprapubic catheter yesterday. Urology did it to reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with a Pseudomonas UTI. A fresh catheter helps clear the source and prevents reinfection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My stomach feels full. I haven’t had a bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows a lot of stool. Colorectal surgery recommends daily tap water enemas and a strong bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had constipation before. It’s hard to manage at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your rehab team knows. They’ll help you keep up with the irrigation and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your hemoglobin dropped a bit after the fluids, but it’s not from bleeding — more likely dilution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. We’re starting iron supplements to help your body make more red blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already take vitamins. Is this different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this is ferrous sulfate — stronger iron. We’ll stop the zinc you were taking, though. It’s usually only for short courses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line today in your arm. It’ll let you get antibiotics outside the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local numbing medicine. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Where will I go after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Short-term rehab. You’ll finish your antibiotics there and work on strength and bowel care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC line is working well. Chest X-ray confirms it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad I won’t need to stay here the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also refilling your baclofen pump today. Chronic Pain Service will do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having more spasms. That’ll help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should reduce stiffness and spasms. We’ll keep your other MS meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count is normal, and you’re off the blood pressure support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re no longer septic. We’re confident the Pseudomonas is being treated effectively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the yeast in my urine? I saw that on the report.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that too. But since you’re not symptomatic, we’re not treating it. It’s common with catheters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow you’ll be discharged to rehab. You’ll continue Zosyn through the PICC for about two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What follow-ups do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infectious disease in two weeks for your UTI history, and ortho for your fracture. We’ll send all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sister — she helps me. Should she know anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll coordinate with her and your rehab center, especially about your baclofen pump refill schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the nicotine patch. It helps with cravings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Keep using it as prescribed. We want to support your efforts to quit smoking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sacral ulcer — is it healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, wound care says it’s clean and healing. Keep taking vitamin C. We’ll monitor the brace site for new pressure areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re going to rehab after I review your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You beat septic shock, your fracture is stable, and your infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. Keep up with the bowel regimen, take your iron, and attend all follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing well. Rehab will help you regain strength and independence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you around if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with advanced multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder with a suprapubic catheter, and a history of recurrent multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections, was admitted due to fever, lethargy, and septic shock. He was found to have a left distal femoral fracture managed non-operatively with a brace. Urine culture grew multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, treated with piperacillin-tazobactam via a PICC line. He stabilized quickly, with resolution of sepsis and ongoing management of constipation, anemia, and pressure ulcers. His baclofen pump was refilled during admission. He was discharged to short-term rehab to complete antibiotics and receive supportive care, with follow-up planned in infectious disease and orthopedics.
